description_full: Colliers International Group Inc. provides commercial real estate, engineering, and investment management solutions in the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia, the United Kingdom, Poland, China, India, and internationally. The company offers capital markets services for property sales, debt finance, mortgage investment banking, and landlord and tenant representation services; and outsourcing services, such as building operations and maintenance, facilities management, lease administration, property accounting and financial reporting, contract and construction management, valuation and appraisal review and management, portfolio or single asset valuation, financial reporting advisory, arbitration consulting, research, highest and best use studies, property tax reviews, appeals and litigation support, and occupier services, as well as loan servicing. It also engages in the planning, designing, and project management of assets, including bridges and structure, highway and traffic engineering, construction engineering and inspection, water, traffic planning, and rail; and provision of air quality assessments, brownfield redevelopment, environmental impact assessments, ground water resource development, site remediation, noise studies, land development and monitoring, and other services, as well as water, storm, and wastewater management services. In addition, the company offers project management services, which include bid document review, construction monitoring and delivery management, contract administration and integrated cost control, development management, facility and engineering functionality, milestone and performance monitoring, quality assurance, risk management and strategic project consulting; and perpetual funds, long-dated funds, and separately managed accounts. Colliers International Group Inc. was founded in 1972 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Jay Stewart Hennick CM | Global Chairman & CEO | Age 68 | Compensation: $5.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 28K people. Revenue per employee of $199K ranks in the bottom quartile among Real Estate peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $9K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 27× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Colliers International Group In is a mid-cap real estate business with a $4.8B market cap on $5.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 8% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $251M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.20× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.2×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 11% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 16pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.33x its revenue share).
It accounts for 1.5% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 42% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 38% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 1.03, it moves roughly with the market.
About $21.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 60% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $39.10 (margin of safety -143%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 58%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.57 to $65.00 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 12.6 vs 16.3, richer on P/E 66.8 vs 23.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 31% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $136 on average, 43% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 8.4%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.74).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.20x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 5%.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.2x net debt to EBITDA ($229.6M of cash against $1.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.56 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
Goodwill makes up 39% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.6% over 3 years, 14.8% over 5 years and 12.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue up 27% and FFO growth of 14.7% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 11.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 84%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.3% (0.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 31.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 28,000 employees, each generates about $199K of revenue, 0.1x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 6.8% a year.
That works out to $9K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.4M (27x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
